/-!
# Erdős Problem 318

*References:*
  - [erdosproblems.com/318](https://www.erdosproblems.com/318)
  - [ErSt75] Erdős, P. and Straus, E. G., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 183.
  - [Sa75] Sattler, R., Solution to Problem 387. Nieuw Arch. Wisk. (1975), 184-189.
  - [Sa82b] Sattler, R., On Erdős property P₁ for the arithmetical sequence. Nederl. Akad. Wetensch.
    Indag. Math. (1982), 347--352.
  - [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
    theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
  - [La26] D. Larsen, [Erdős problem 318](https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-318/blob/main/318.pdf) (2026)
-/

open Set Real

namespace Erdos318

/-- A set `A : Set ℕ` is said to have property `P₁` if for any nonconstant sequence
`f : A → {-1, 1}`, one can always select a finite, nonempty subset `S ⊆ A \ {0}` such that
`∑ n ∈ S, fₙ / n = 0`. This is defined in [Sa82b]. -/
def P₁ (A : Set ℕ) : Prop := ∀ (f : ℕ → ℝ),
  f ∘ (Subtype.val : (A \ {0} : Set ℕ) → ℕ) ≠ (fun _ => 1) →
  f ∘ (Subtype.val : (A \ {0} : Set ℕ) → ℕ) ≠ (fun _ => - 1) →
  Set.range f ⊆ {1, -1} →
  ∃ S : Finset ℕ, S.Nonempty ∧ ↑S ⊆ A \ {0} ∧ ∑ n ∈ S, f n / n = 0

/-- `ℕ` has property `P₁`. This is proved in [ErSt75]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.univ : P₁ univ := by
  sorry

/-- Sattler proved in [Sa75] that the set of odd numbers has property `P₁`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.odd : P₁ {n | Odd n} := by
  sorry

/-- The set of squares does not have property `P₁`. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.squares : ¬ P₁ ({n | IsSquare n}) := by
  simp only [P₁, not_forall, not_exists, not_and]
  -- Consider the function `f` that sends `1` to `1` and sends all other numbers to `-1`.
  refine ⟨fun n => if n = 1 then 1 else - 1, fun h => ?_, fun h => ?_,
    fun x ⟨y, hy⟩ => ?_, fun S h hs => ?_⟩
  · have : (- 1 : ℝ) = 1 := by simpa using congr_fun h ⟨4, ⟨⟨2, by grind⟩, by grind⟩⟩
    grind
  · have : 1 = (- 1 : ℝ) := by simpa using congr_fun h ⟨1, ⟨IsSquare.one, by grind⟩⟩
    grind
  · by_cases x = 1 <;> grind
  -- Consider two cases: `1 ∈ S` or `1 ∉ S`. In the first case, the finite sum over `S` is bounded
  -- below by `1 - (π ^ 2 / 6 - 1)`, which is positive. In the second case, the finite sum over `S`
  -- is negative.
  by_cases h1 : 1 ∈ S
  · rw [Finset.sum_eq_add_sum_sdiff_singleton 1 _ (by simp [h1]), Finset.sum_congr rfl
      (g := fun n : ℕ => (- 1 : ℝ) / n)]
    · simp only [↓reduceIte, Nat.cast_one, div_self one_ne_zero, ← ne_eq, div_eq_mul_one_div
        (- 1 : ℝ), ← Finset.mul_sum, neg_one_mul (∑ x ∈ S \ {1}, 1 / (x : ℝ)), ← sub_eq_add_neg]
      apply ne_of_gt
      calc
      _ < 1 - (π ^ 2 / 6 - 1) := by
        have : π ^ 2 < 3.15 ^ 2 := by gcongr; exact Real.pi_lt_d2
        linarith
      _ = 1 - (∑' n : ℕ, 1 / (n : ℝ) ^ 2 - 1) := by congr; exact hasSum_zeta_two.tsum_eq.symm
      _ ≤ 1 - ∑ n ∈ S \ {1}, 1 / (n : ℝ) := by
        gcongr
        have : 1 = 1 / ((1 : ℕ) : ℝ) := by norm_cast; grind
        nth_rewrite 3 [this]
        rw [le_sub_iff_add_le, ← Finset.sum_eq_sum_sdiff_singleton_add h1]
        let S' := S.preimage (· ^ 2) (Function.Injective.injOn
          (Nat.pow_left_injective (by decide)))
        have hS' : S'.map ⟨(· ^ 2), Nat.pow_left_injective (by decide)⟩ = S := by
          apply Finset.coe_injective
          have h : (S : Set ℕ) ⊆ Set.range (· ^ 2) :=
            hs.trans (by simp [isSquare_iff_exists_sq, Set.subset_def])
          simpa [S', Set.image_preimage_eq_iff] using h
        rw [← hS', Finset.sum_map, Function.Embedding.coeFn_mk]
        simpa [Nat.cast_pow] using Summable.sum_le_tsum S' (fun _ _ => by positivity) (by simp)
    · intro _ _; grind
  · suffices ∑ n ∈ S, (fun n ↦ if n = 1 then 1 else - 1) n / (n : ℝ) < 0 from by linarith
    refine Finset.sum_neg (fun p hp => ?_) h
    have : p ≠ 1 := by grind
    simp_all [neg_div, zero_lt_iff, (not_iff_not.2 mem_singleton_iff).1 (hs hp).2]

/-- For any set `A` containing exactly one even number, `A` does not have property `P₁`. Sattler
[Sa82] credits this observation to Erdős, who presumably found this after [ErGr80]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even {A : Set ℕ} (hA : {n | n ∈ A ∧ Even n}.ncard = 1) :
    ¬ P₁ A := by
  sorry

/-- There exists a set `A` with positive density that does not have property `P₁`.
#TODO: prove this lemma by assuming `erdos_318.contain_single_even`.

The density sits in an existential, so `HasPosDensity` is the *stronger* reading here and
weakening it to positive lower density would claim less, which is the opposite of the usual
situation for Erdős' "positive density". It also costs nothing: by
`erdos_318.variants.contain_single_even` a witness only needs exactly one even element, and the
odd numbers together with one even number have density `1 / 2` on the nose. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.parts.i : ∃ A : Set ℕ, HasPosDensity A ∧ ¬ P₁ A := by
  sorry

/-- Every infinite arithmetic progression has property `P₁`. This is proved in [Sa82b]. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.variants.infinite_AP {A : Set ℕ} (hA : A.IsAPOfLength ⊤) : P₁ A := by
  sorry

/--
Does the set of squares excluding 1 have property `P₁`?

Larsen [La26] proved that this set does have property `P₁`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_318.parts.ii : answer(True) ↔  P₁ ({n | IsSquare n} \ {1}) := by
  sorry

end Erdos318

findings.description: The theorem lacks an infinitude or nontriviality assumption on A. Take A = {2}. Its even-member set has ncard = 1, but P₁ {2} is true: every sign-valued function is constant on the singleton, so the two nonconstancy premises cannot both hold. Thus this instance of the conclusion is false. The scratch file proves P₁ {a} for every natural a and refutes the universally quantified single-even statement without using any sorry-backed theorem.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/318 presents the single-even observation in the discussion of infinite denominator sets and the question about sets of positive density. Erdős–Graham, Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory (1980), p. 42, likewise discusses infinite sign sequences indexed by k = 1, 2, … and asks about denominator sets of positive density. Singletons fall outside this setting and have no nonconstant sign assignment.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `(hInf : A.Infinite)`, or minimally `(A \ {0}).Nontrivial`. This must be combined with the separate correction to the counting of zero described below.

findings.description: The hypothesis counts zero as an even member, although P₁ removes zero from both the sign-function domain and the permitted denominators. Let A = insert 0 {n : ℕ | Odd n}. This set is infinite and its unique even member is 0, so hA holds. However, its positive part is precisely the odd numbers, giving P₁ A ↔ P₁ {n | Odd n}; the latter is the known positive result of Sattler. Consequently the conclusion is false even after adding an infinitude hypothesis. The scratch file verifies the cardinality, infinitude, and invariance of P₁ under inserting zero.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Graham (1980), p. 42, uses positive reciprocal denominators. https://www.erdosproblems.com/318 explicitly records that Sattler [Sa75] proved the property for the odd numbers. The unique-even obstruction concerns an actual positive even denominator, not zero, which contributes no permitted term in this formalization.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace hA by `(hA : {n | n ∈ A \ {0} ∧ Even n}.ncard = 1)`, or add `(hpos : 0 ∉ A)` to the current hypothesis. Retain the infinitude/nontriviality guard needed for the singleton issue.

findings.description: The docstring requires a nonconstant function on A, but the Lean definition requires nonconstancy on A \ {0}. These differ when zero belongs to A. For A = {0,1}, the Lean predicate is true vacuously, while the documented property is false: assign opposite signs at 0 and 1; the only allowed nonempty subset of A \ {0} is {1}, whose signed reciprocal is nonzero. This discrepancy is proved in the scratch file. The Lean definition's positive-domain interpretation itself matches the source.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Graham (1980), p. 42, starts the sign sequence at k = 1, and https://www.erdosproblems.com/318 tests nonconstancy on the denominator set. In the Lean representation that set is A \ {0}, rather than all of A.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to describe a nonconstant `f : (A \ {0}) → {-1, 1}`, or explicitly say that the restriction to A \ {0} must be nonconstant.

reformulations.difference: Lean quantifies over global real-valued functions whose entire range lies in {1,-1}, rather than functions defined only on the positive denominator set. It expresses nonconstancy by excluding the two constant sign functions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Restriction to the positive part gives a source sign assignment. Conversely, any assignment there extends to all naturals by assigning 1 outside the set. For sign-valued functions, exclusion of both constant functions is equivalent to occurrence of both signs. The scratch lemmas signs_iff and p1_iff_local prove equivalence with a formulation that constrains values only on A \ {0} and explicitly requires both signs there.

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether the property holds for arbitrary positive-density sets; Lean records the negative answer as an existential counterexample and requires an existing positive natural density.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Negating the universal assertion gives the existential counterexample formulation. Requiring an existing natural density does not change the answer here: the odd numbers together with 2 have density exactly 1/2 and fail P₁. Give 2 the positive sign and every odd denominator the negative sign. A sum omitting 2 is negative; a sum including 2 cannot vanish because a finite sum of reciprocals of odd numbers has odd denominator and cannot equal 1/2. This witness also satisfies positive lower or upper density readings.

reformulations.difference: The set expression syntactically contains zero, and the conclusion uses one nonempty vanishing signed sum rather than Larsen's two nonempty finite subsets with equal reciprocal sums.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: P₁ removes zero, so the effective set is exactly the perfect squares greater than 1; this set identity and the corresponding P₁ equivalence are proved in the scratch file. A nonconstant sign assignment gives a partition into two nonempty sign classes. Splitting a vanishing sum by sign gives equal reciprocal sums, and positivity of every denominator forces both selected parts to be nonempty. Conversely, the union of Larsen's two selected parts gives the required vanishing signed sum. The full partition equivalence was checked mathematically, not formalized.

submission.summary: Added an infinitude hypothesis and restricted the single-even cardinality condition to positive members of A, excluding both reported counterexamples. Updated the corresponding docstrings and density-witness comment, including the trivial P₁ docstring correction.
